blocks.text: 前沿模型的能力正在快速提升，而我们理解、对齐并保障其安全的能力必须始终领先一步。我们正在控制模型的开发与发布节奏，包括在需要更多时间达到安全标准时暂停内部训练⁠（在新窗口打开），或暂缓发布 GPT‑6.1 Astra 等模型。我们引入了安全案例等新流程，并要求在整个训练过程中提供更有力的对齐行为证据。这些要求会拖慢模型发布的速度，但也让我们更有信心安全地向前推进。

blocks.text: 自 7 月发生 Hugging Face 事件⁠以来，我们加强了模型训练、测试和部署环节的防护措施与对齐要求。本文说明我们在每个阶段如何评估和管理风险，从高度隔离的训练环境，到你在自己电脑上使用的 Codex 部署。我们在每个阶段都会评估模型和防护措施，必须通过安全审查才能进入下一阶段。

inlines.text: 自 7 月发生
Hugging Face 事件⁠

blocks.text: 覆盖模型全生命周期的纵深防御

inlines.text: 覆盖模型全生命周期的纵深防御

blocks.text: 我们采用纵深防御策略，设置多层保护，以降低对任何单一防护措施的依赖。如果某一层失效，其他层可以协助防止伤害、限制后果，或向我们发出警报以便介入。

blocks.text: 模型对齐

inlines.text: 模型对齐

blocks.text: 对齐是指让 AI 系统可靠地按照我们的意图行事。模型必须理解用户的需求，同时遵守政策以及更广泛的社会利益。我们训练模型遵循模型规范⁠中的原则，并通过对齐评估、审计以及更广泛部署前的审查来评估其表现。

blocks.text: 安全与沙箱隔离

inlines.text: 安全与沙箱隔离

blocks.text: 这些控制措施限制模型可以访问或影响的文件、工具、网络及其他资源，有助于在训练和评估期间控制错误或不对齐行为造成的后果。

inlines.text: 这些控制措施限制模型可以访问或影响的文件、工具、网络及其他资源，有助于在训练和评估期间控制错误或不对齐行为造成的后果。

blocks.text: 拦截式防护

inlines.text: 拦截式防护

blocks.text: 这些是额外的防护措施，通过评估用户请求和模型操作，拦截可能有害或未经授权的行为。其中包括帮助防止网络滥用或协助制造生物武器的安全分类器⁠（在新窗口打开），以及可以拦截潜在未经授权模型操作的自动审查⁠（在新窗口打开）。

blocks.text: 监控与响应

inlines.text: 监控与响应

blocks.text: 这些系统负责发现可疑行为、调查事件经过，并在需要时介入。它们提供部署流量的可见性，并能就新出现的风险类型向我们发出警报。

inlines.text: 这些系统负责发现可疑行为、调查事件经过，并在需要时介入。它们提供部署流量的可见性，并能就新出现的风险类型向我们发出警报。

blocks.text: 有效的监控取决于模型可监控性，即监控系统能否可靠地从模型的推理和操作中发现错误或不安全行为。例如，一个在思维链（CoT）中说出自己作弊意图的模型，比一个隐瞒这一信息的模型更容易被监控。我们在训练期间和部署前评估可监控性，开发更好的衡量方法⁠（在新窗口打开），并研究影响它的因素⁠（在新窗口打开）。

blocks.text: 在模型开发与部署的三个阶段中，每一层的作用各不相同：

inlines.text: 在模型开发与部署的三个阶段中，每一层的作用各不相同：
研究：
我们在沙箱环境中训练、测试和使用模型。
内部部署：
OpenAI 员工将模型用于实际工作。
外部部署：
模型向更广泛的人群和组织开放。

blocks.text: 不同阶段我们依赖的防护层也不同。训练期间，对齐尚不确定，我们更倚重沙箱和监控。随着模型在部署阶段获得更广泛的访问权限，对齐和系统级控制变得越来越重要。在每个阶段，我们都会评估各项防护措施合在一起，是否足以匹配模型的能力和访问权限。我们的判断可能会由安全咨询小组（SAG）复核，并接受 OpenAI 基金会董事会安全与安保委员会（SSC）的监督。

blocks.text: 研究期间：将模型限制在沙箱环境中

inlines.text: 研究期间：将模型限制在沙箱环境中

blocks.text: 在研究阶段，我们通过评估模型来建立对其对齐属性的信心。由于目前还不能完全依靠对齐来防止危害，我们高度依赖安全和沙箱机制，限制模型能访问和操作的范围。

blocks.text: 我们持续对这一系统进行红队测试，让由我们最强模型组成的团队尝试接入实时互联网、突破安全边界，或与它们本应隔离的智能体通信。这有助于检验防护措施能否抵御其要约束的模型能力。

blocks.text: 作为额外的防御层，我们监控所有前沿推理，以检测模型是否绕过了我们的安全不变量。如果监控发现模型已接入互联网，我们会呼叫安全团队并自动暂停该工作负载。

blocks.text: 当防护失效时，监控提供了关键的兜底。在最近一份失准报告中，我们披露监控曾发现一个内部研究模型利用 DNS 配置错误⁠（在新窗口中打开）获得了有限的互联网访问。9 月 20 日至 10 月 1 日期间，我们暂停了最强模型的训练和评估，同时调查并修复了这一安全缺口。

blocks.text: 为了让干预快速可靠，我们构建了 Control Room⁠，这是一个集中式系统，可跟踪研究工作负载，并在收到停止作业指令后 35 秒内停止模型的进一步输出。这些控制直接在推理基础设施中强制执行，因此不依赖每个研究工作负载自行实现关停机制。对于前沿模型研究工作负载，如果 Control Room 不可用，它们也会停止模型输出。

blocks.text: 红队测试与监控相辅相成。我们无法保证沙箱牢不可破，但红队测试能帮我们评估模型需要付出多大代价才能逃逸。模型所需的代价越高，监控方发现并阻止它的机会就越大。

inlines.text: 红队测试与监控相辅相成。我们无法保证沙箱牢不可破，但红队测试能帮我们评估模型需要付出多大代价才能逃逸。模型所需的代价越高，监控方发现并阻止它的机会就越大。

blocks.text: 我们在研究阶段强制实施严格的安全与监控措施，原因有以下几点：

inlines.text: 我们在研究阶段强制实施严格的安全与监控措施，原因有以下几点：
模型仍在评估中。
部分模型尚未完成公开发布所需的安全训练、对齐审计和审查。
**前沿研究环境可能放大风险。**某些研究任务需要更宏大的设置，使模型比外部部署时通常表现得更执着、能力更强（例如，解决
纳维-斯托克斯问题
需要一支由 10,000 个智能体组成的团队）。
大规模训练时人工监督更少。
与典型的 Codex 会话不同，我们的训练工作负载涉及大量模型操作，没有专人逐一跟进每次交互。

blocks.text: 在这一阶段，我们让模型访问更广泛的互联网、我们的 Slack、代码库和内部基础设施。这是风险上的重大变化，因为模型的行为现在会直接影响我们构建和运行 OpenAI 所用的系统。在内部部署期间，我们需要更多地依赖模型对齐、系统防护和监控，而非安全控制。

对前沿模型，这包括用内部自动化红队开展新一轮
自适应测试
，对模型的稳健性进行压力测试。我们在
系统卡（在新窗口打开）
中公布能力与安全评估的结果。
对能力最强的模型，我们还会请第三方参与测试
，对防滥用措施和模型本身的对齐情况进行压力测试。
检查内部部署阶段的监控标记
，追踪基础模型底层对齐状况的任何变化。

blocks.text: 除了“同步”防护措施（例如模型安全训练和系统分类器），外部部署还依赖离线执法与调查。这些团队结合规模化智能体调查员与人工审核，识别并锁定潜在威胁行为者，涵盖网络滥用、生物武器化、蒸馏以及模型自身的失准等问题。离线执法尤其有助于跨账号收集信息，从而更全面地勾勒潜在威胁。

blocks.text: 当我们发现某一层安全防护出现失效时，无论是否实际造成伤害，都希望迅速调查、分级，并在可行且适当的情况下对外披露。按照我们的失准报告政策，任何员工都可以标记事件并要求公开披露。这些报告会被调查；如果在是否应对外披露上存在分歧，决定将上报至我们的安全咨询小组（SAG）。除了依赖员工报告，我们还会主动查找失准事件，以便处理并分享发现。

blocks.text: The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating, and our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead. We are pacing the development and release of our models, including pausinginternal training⁠(opens in a new window) or holding back models like GPT‑6.1 Astra when we need more time to meet our safety standards. We’ve introduced new processes such as safety cases and require stronger evidence of aligned behavior throughout training. These requirements slow the pace of model releases, but they give us greater confidence to safely move forward.

blocks.text: Since the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July, we've strengthened safeguards and alignment requirements for how we train, test, and deploy models. This post explains how we evaluate and manage risk at each stage, from highly sandboxed training environments to the Codex deployment you use on your computer. We evaluate both models and safeguards at each stage, requiring a safety review to advance to the next stage.

blocks.text: Model alignment

inlines.text: Model alignment

blocks.text: Alignment is about making AI systems reliably act in ways we intend. Models must interpret what users want while also respecting policies, and broader societal interests. We train our models to align to the principles in theModel Spec⁠. We assess how well they do this through alignment evaluations, auditing, and review before broader deployment.

blocks.text: Monitoring and response

inlines.text: Monitoring and response

blocks.text: These systems detect concerning behavior, investigate what happened, and intervene when needed. They provide visibility of deployment traffic, and can alert us to new emerging types of risks.

inlines.text: These systems detect concerning behavior, investigate what happened, and intervene when needed. They provide visibility of deployment traffic, and can alert us to new emerging types of risks.

blocks.text: Effective monitoring depends on model monitorability - how reliably monitors can detect mistakes or unsafe behavior from a model’s reasoning and actions. For example, a model that verbalizes its intention to cheat in its chain-of-thought (CoT) is more monitorable than one that omits this information. We evaluate monitorability during training and before deployment, develop better methods for measuring⁠(opens in a new window) it, and study what affects it⁠(opens in a new window).

blocks.text: The role of each layer changes across three stages of model development and deployment:

inlines.text: The role of each layer changes across three stages of model development and deployment:
Research:
We train, test, and use models in sandboxed environments.
Internal deployment:
OpenAI employees use models for practical work.
External deployment:
Models become available to people and organizations more broadly.

blocks.text: We rely on different layers at different stages. During training, when alignment is less certain, we depend more heavily on sandboxing and monitoring. As models gain broader access during deployment, alignment and system-level controls become increasingly important. At each stage, we evaluate whether the combined protections are sufficient for the model’s capabilities and access. Our determinations may be reviewed with our Safety Advisory Group (SAG) and overseen by the Safety and Security Committee (SSC) of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board of Directors.

blocks.text: Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no live internet access. After the Hugging Face incident, we significantly restructured our internal research systems to contain models using:

blocks.text: We continuously red-team this system, having teams of our strongest models try to reach the live internet, escape security boundaries, or communicate with agents they are meant to be isolated from. This helps us test whether containment holds against the capabilities of the models it is intended to constrain.

blocks.text: Monitoring provides a critical backstop when containment fails. In a recent misalignment report, we shared that monitorsdetected an internal research model exploiting a DNS misconfiguration⁠(opens in a new window) to gain limited internet access. We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models from September 20th to October 1st while we investigated and addressed the security gap.

blocks.text: To make interventions fast and reliable, we built Control Room⁠, a central system that tracks research workloads and stops further model output within 35 seconds of receiving an instruction to halt a job. These controls are enforced directly in the inference infrastructure, so they do not depend on each research workload implementing its own shutdown mechanism. For frontier-model research workloads, they also stop model output if Control Room becomes unavailable.

blocks.text: Red-teaming and monitoring work together. We cannot guarantee that a sandbox is impenetrable, but red-teaming helps us assess how much effort a model would need to escape it. The more effort the model requires, the more the opportunity for monitors to detect and stop it.

Navier Stokes problem
Training runs at scale with less direct human oversight.
Unlike a typical Codex session, o ur training workloads involve large numbers of model actions without a person following each interaction.

This gives us a better understanding of how the models behave in practical settings⁠(opens in a new window), and informs deployment decisions.

blocks.text: During this phase, we give the model access to the broader internet, our Slack, our codebase, and internal infrastructure. This is a significant change in risk, as the model’s actions now have a direct impact on the systems we use to build and run OpenAI. During internal deployment, we need to rely more on model alignment, system safeguards, and monitoring as opposed to security controls.

This is a significant change in risk, as the model’s actions now have a direct impact on the systems we use to build and run OpenAI. During internal deployment, we need to rely more on model alignment, system safeguards, and monitoring as opposed to security controls.

blocks.text: Before a frontier model can be deployed outside of the sandbox, it must first go through alignment and monitorability testing⁠(opens in a new window). We have a suite of alignment evaluations, which test both for specific alignment failure modes (such as circumventing safety and security restrictions) and broad measurements of propensity (such as resampling internal Codex trajectories and checking for misalignment). You can see more about our alignment and monitorability evaluations in the latest GPT‑6 Astra system card⁠(opens in a new window).

We also generally require Auto-Review⁠(opens in a new window) for employees using Codex, which evaluates potentially risk actions and escalates them back to the user.

blocks.text: Finally, we monitor for misaligned behavior on every frontier inference during internal deployment. Monitoring also helps us investigate new forms of misalignment⁠(opens in a new window).

inlines.text: External deployment: protect against misuse and misalignment at scale

blocks.text: Public deployment exposes models to far more users, tasks, and environments, increasing both the scale and variety of risks. At this stage, we also need to protect against potentially malicious actors who purposefully direct the model to perform harm.

blocks.text: Before public release, models and system safeguards must meet our external deployment safety requirements. We assess them through:

inlines.text: Before public release, models and system safeguards must meet our external deployment safety requirements. We assess them through:
Performing a larger suite of alignment and safety evaluations.
For our frontier models, this includes performing new rounds of
adaptive testing⁠
with our internal automated redteamers to stress-test the robustness of the model. We publish the results of our capability and safety evaluations in our
system cards⁠(opens in a new window)
For our most capable models, we also perform testing with third parties
to stress-test both our safeguards against misuse and the underlying alignment of our models.
Examining monitoring flags from the internal deployment stage
to track any changes in the base model’s underlying alignment.

blocks.text: In addition to our “synchronous” safeguards (such as model safety training and system classifiers), for external deployments we also leverage offline enforcement and investigation. These teams use a combination of scaled agentic investigators and human review to detect and identify potential threat actors, ranging from cyberabuse, bioweaponization, distillation⁠, and misalignment from the model itself. Offline enforcement is especially helpful to gather information across accounts in order to build a more holistic picture of a potential threat.

blocks.text: Incident Response and Disclosure

inlines.text: Incident Response and Disclosure

blocks.text: When we notice a failure in one of our layers of safety, regardless of whether any harm actually occurred, we want to quickly investigate, triage, and if possible and appropriate, disclose the failure externally. Under our misalignment reporting⁠ policy, any employee can flag an incident for public disclosure. These reports are investigated, and if there is a disagreement on whether they should be externally disclosed, the decision is escalated to our Safety Advisory Group (SAG). In addition to relying on employee reports, we proactively look for misalignment incidents so we can address them and share findings.

blocks.text: This work depends on both research progress and operational discipline: configuring controls correctly, testing how they interact, and responding decisively when they fail. A misconfigured network service or a failed automatic stop can undermine otherwise strong protections.

blocks.text: As models gain new capabilities, we will need to keep challenging the assumptions behind our safeguards and improving them where necessary. Lessons from research, internal use, and public deployment must inform how we train, evaluate, and deploy the next models.

blocks.text: We will continue sharing findings through system cards, incident reports, internal deployment risk reports⁠(opens in a new window), and external evaluations⁠ so that others can scrutinize our approach, including its limitations. When that evidence falls short of the bar we hold for safety, we will again pause training or withhold release until those requirements are met.

inlines.text: Setting safety standards
Pacing model development in an era of cyber-critical capabilities
— How we slowed frontier training while strengthening containment, expanding monitoring, and requiring stronger evidence of alignment.
Towards safety cases for frontier AI training
— Initial guidelines for evidence-based safety arguments covering technical safeguards, operational practices, and investigations of misalignment.
Priorities and principles for effective third party assessments
— Our proposed approach to independent scrutiny of safety cases, safeguards, evaluations, and model behavior.
Periodic Summary of Internal Use Catastrophic-Risk Assessments
⁠(opens in a new window)
— Our public report covering June–September 2026 describes internal frontier-model deployments, their assessed risks, and changes to safeguards and governance.

blocks.text: Defining and evaluating aligned behavior

inlines.text: Defining and evaluating aligned behavior
An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI
— How we updated the Model Spec around five core values to guide models’ judgment, behavior, and respect for human oversight.
Eval-production behavior gaps in agent safety and the role of eval-awareness
⁠(opens in a new window)
— A study of differences between safety-evaluation results and production behavior, including how models’ interpretations of evaluation objectives affect performance.
Beyond g-mean²: complementary metrics for monitorability
⁠(opens in a new window)
— New metrics for comparing monitorability and estimating residual risk in simulated systems where monitors reject model outputs.
GPT‑6 Astra System Card
⁠(opens in a new window)
— Detailed evaluations of Astra’s capabilities, safety, alignment, and monitorability, alongside its deployment safeguards and limitations.

blocks.text: Containing models and improving safeguards

inlines.text: Containing models and improving safeguards
Securing our frontier model training environment
— How we strengthened isolation, built offline research environments, and used our strongest models to test containment boundaries.
Training activation classifiers for safety and alignment
⁠(opens in a new window)
— How classifiers use models’ internal activations to detect potentially harmful behavior and interrupt responses or tool calls.
Auto-review of agent actions without synchronous human oversight
⁠(opens in a new window)
— How a separate review agent assesses actions that cross sandbox boundaries, helping coding agents work autonomously while blocking potentially harmful or unauthorized actions.
GPT‑Red: Unlocking Self-Improvement for Robustness
— How we train automated red-teamers through self-play to discover vulnerabilities and improve models’ robustness against prompt injections.
Control Room
— How we track workloads across our research infrastructure and enforce rapid stops to model output when safety or security concerns require intervention.

How we detect frontier model misalignment
— Our monitoring system combines activation probes, model-based review, automated investigation, and human response to detect and investigate concerning behavior.
The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead
— Our findings from the Hugging Face incident and the changes it prompted across security, monitoring, and alignment.
An agent used DNS to reach an external chatbot
⁠(opens in a new window)

Disrupting a coordinated model-distillation campaign

Our framework for reporting model misalignment
